speechtext:

On December 24 last, the office of the Minister of Labour called for the government JetStar to come to Hamilton at about 4 p.m. to take the minister to Sault Ste. Marie. Because of weather conditions they could not land in Sault Ste. Marie and had to land in Toronto. speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: LANDING OF SOVIET SATELLITE ON CANADIAN SOIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister and it refers to reports of a Soviet satellite which apparently descended in the Great Slave Lake area today. We understand that the Prime Minister was advised of this matter by an early morning telephone call from the President of the United States.
This seems to raise a very important question touching Canadian sovereignty. Canada is supposed to be an equal partner in the NORAD arrangement which would be surveying the movement of this kind of vehicle into Canadian orbit. Since Canada is an equal partner in NORAD, why was the Prime Minister of Canada not advised by Canadian officials about this penetration of Canadian territory; and if he was not advised by Canadian officials, does that indicate that the only way Canada becomes informed of possible threats to itself is by telephone calls from American officials?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CONTENT OF PIPE TO BE MANUFACTURED FOR NORTHERN PIPELINE-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring the Prime Minister back to earth. The Deputy Prime Minister said in Ottawa on September 9 that 100,000 man-years of employment would be created-that is a phrase right out of his press release-not "might be" or "could be", but would be created in Canada as a direct result of the construction of the Alcan pipeline. When we asked an officer of the pipeline company what this figure was based on, we were told it was based on the assumption that Canada would produce 98 per cent of the pipe for the Canadian section of the pipeline.
My question to the Prime Minister is as follows. Considering that the Deputy Prime Minister yesterday, both in the House and, if I understood it correctly, outside the House, withdrew the government's promise to produce 98 per cent of the pipe in Canada, and therefore withdrew entirely the very specific commitment to produce the 100,000 man-years of employment which he categorically promised on September 9, does this turnaround by the Deputy Prime Minister reflect government policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
that Bill C-18, to amend the Anti-Inflation Act and guidelines, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-18 is now before the House for second reading. Some of the amendments in this bill are for housekeeping purposes and have been required for some time. Others are needed to ensure that the decontrol process will be orderly.

January 24, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
Controls were never intended to be permanent since this government does not believe in excessive intervention in the market place. Last October I announced that a phased process of decontrol would begin on April 14 of this year. We believe that this date will ensure that wage and price controls will be in place for the right length of time. Most groups and firms will remain subject to the guidelines until the last quarter of 1978.
The recent high rates of increase in inflation have resulted mainly from food prices and the depreciation of the exchange rate. I am confident that almost all of the impact of these developments is now behind us and that inflation will trend downward during 1978. Wage increases have been coming in at more reasonable levels and the AIB's price prenotification program is indicating only moderate changes.
Part of our progress is being made by a shift in attitudes. There is now a widespread recognition that we cannot expect the economy to deliver the large increases in real income which we enjoyed in the easy times of the 1960s and early 1970s. There is a better understanding of our goals and priorities and, in particular, of the difficulties involved in maintaining a competitive international trading position.

Our prospects are improving with regard to salary costs. The number of work days lost as a result of strikes decreased considerably last year. Union leaders have indicated that wage claims will be reasonable after April 14. All understand that unrealistic demand will only tend to reduce job creation or lead to the disappearance of existing ones. Public authorities, at every level, are showing more discipline than a few years ago.
Various new steps are being taken, as we near the phasing-out of controls. Our wage policy will guarantee that the state, as an employer, will not provoke in the private sector such wage increases as might be likely to stir a flare up in wages and prices. The federal-provincial conference of the finance ministers, to be held this week will give me a chance to broach this subject with my provincial counterparts, as well as with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) in the hope that a similar policy might be implemented throughout the public sector.
I plan to announce in the near future the details of the setting up of a control body whose main mission will be to see to it that all groups remain aware of the ravages of inflation, and draw attention to such inflationary elements as may exist. [English]
Let me now turn to the specific clauses of this bill. Two of the amendments relate to the decontrol process. The first of these was introduced last summer. It would deem compensation plans to be amended in line with a recommendation of the AIB or an order of the administrator. Without this amendment, groups would probably be entitled to the negotiated level of wages as soon as controls cease to apply.
The other deals with administration in the transition period and prevents the use of what are known as AIB clauses. As the
[Mr. Chritien.l
act now stands, no action can be taken against those firms or groups who have not reported early enough to allow a binding order to be issued by the administrator prior to December 31, 1978. This situation is clearly unsatisfactory and inequitable. This amendment would ensure that reports would be filed for the period covered by controls and allow the AIB, the administrator and the Anti-Inflation Appeal Tribunal to remain in operation as long as necessary to enforce compliance in respect of the controls period.
With respect to the "AIB clauses", the amendment will prevent the use of clauses which call for a higher entitlement to compensation as soon as the group is no longer covered by controls. It is designed to build in further restraint against a possible wage bulge.
All but one of the remaining amendments were introduced in Bill C-59 last summer. To review an order in council, which brought various groups that bargain in association under mandatory controls, would be backdated to December 16, 1975. A time limit would be imposed for parties referring a matter to the administrator following a notification from the AIB. The authority of the administrator to issue orders dealing with past or current contraventions of the guidelines would be clarified. Cabinet would be given adequate time to deal with petitions from parties affected by an order of the administrator. The remaining amendment, introduced for the first time, would clarify the definition of compensation plans.

Hon. members in this House will surely see the importance of this bill. It is therefore imperative that we proceed with its study without delay if we want the controls to be lifted in an orderly fashion. Let us not forget that we have little time left before phasing out of the controls begins.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was intrigued by the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who blames food prices and exchange rates for the continuing inflation which Canada is experiencing just now. Blaming food prices is almost the same as saying that the controls program does not work at all. Food prices at the farm gate were not supposed to be controlled. At the other end of the food chain, prices were supposed to be controlled except of course it was not price controls at all that we had, it was profit control. Therefore, any increase in costs could be passed right through to the consumer, and naturally we are not going to have any control over food prices. Long before this anti-inflation program was introduced in the first place the government knew that food prices were a villain and should be controlled.
As far as blaming exchange rates is concerned, Mr. Speaker, the government is responsible in large measure, if not totally, for the situation of exchange rates and the Canadian dollar. After all the government has allowed the productivity of this country to drop at such a rate, compared to other producing countries, that the world markets have finally realized the
January 24, 1978

value of our dollar, and they have placed a proper value on it. That is the reason for the decline in exchange rates.
As for the minister's further remark that the economy cannot deliver the large increases to workers that it used to, we can look to the policies of the present administration and determine that they have in no way encouraged the economy to deliver anything close to what the economy is capable of delivering. For anyone wanting to improve the Canadian economy the government has provided only disincentives.
The minister also remarked that Bill C-18 is mainly a housekeeping bill. We might say that it is about time that the government started doing some housekeeping.
I would like to remind the House of some of the bungling that this government has done during the past few years, particularly in the case of the anti-inflation legislation which has been before the House, but not limited to that. For example, in 1975 we had Bill C-73, the original anti-inflation bill. Then, it was barely five months later the government found that it had to have amendments to the original program. Therefore, in May, 1976, we had Bill C-89, which amended Bill C-73. Then, a little over a year later, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-59 was introduced in July, 1977. Unfortunately the government did not think that Bill C-59 had sufficient priority and it died on the order paper at the end of the session. Now it is six months later and we have another set of Anti-Inflation Act amendments.
I have mentioned bungling, Mr. Speaker, and you may wonder if these are the only examples I have. On the legislative side I would like to refer to the Income Tax Act amendments. We dealt with those not so long ago and the minister and the government members were complaining that the opposition was stonewalling or delaying passage of the legislation. The delay came on the other side of the House, Mr. Speaker. The evidence is clear that Bill C-ll was first debated on November 7, 1977, and only five weeks elapsed between the start of the debate and the passage of the bill. Compare that with the 31 weeks which elapsed between the March 31 budget and the start of debate on the bill. The government left debate of that bill for so long that once again it found it imperative to introduce closure, and the people of Canada were denied a proper debate on another important tax bill. It is known widely that budget bills have effect from the date of the budget and there was absolutely no need for a closure motion to be used in that particular instance.
If that were not enough evidence, I would like to remind the House that even though ten years ago the government knew Bank Act legislation would be needed, we had an introduction yesterday of second reading of the Bank Act amending bill, in spite of the fact that the debate on an initial extension bill passed last year. The debate on that bill continued for a shorter period of time than the bells rang last evening to call a vote on this bill for which they obviously were not ready. What has happened to the proper legislation? That is the kind of bungling that we can do without.
It seems to me the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is appealing to Canadians on the basis that he is not going to run the
Anti-Inflation Act
next election campaign on his record. He cannot, of course, because he doesn't have a good one, so he is going to run the next election based on the future. He thinks Canadians are going to forgive him for his bungling; that is his premise. I say yes, Mr. Speaker, Canadians could easily forgive the government for bungling, but I doubt very much that Canadians are going to forgive the government for its dishonesty.
I would like to skim over a few examples which I suggest are examples of dishonesty on the part of this government. Just last week in the Vancouver newspapers there was an announcement made of the fact that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford)-I am glad he has returned to hear about it- gave the city of Vancouver $200,000 as the first installment of a $400,000 urban demonstration fund grant for the Gastown Fishermen's Wharf. Of course, the people of Vancouver welcomed that kind of participation by the government. But, it is totally dishonest to say that the Minister of Justice gave the city of Vancouver $200,000 as if it were something that he dug out of the Liberal coffers or his own pockets.
The people of Vancouver know where that money came from. It came out of the pockets of the residents of British Columbia. For this government to say that it has given money to the city of Vancouver is dishonest. The article goes on to say that the money came from a $6 million fund originally set aside for use during the United Nations Habitat Conference, but which was not used. Well, what do we take from that? That is an admission that either the government did some very bad budgeting and overprovided $6 million for the Habitat conference, or it had not sufficiently promoted the conference to make it a success and the money was not spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Of course. I was there. I was a delegate. I am aware that the minister's office generated a half million dollar loss as a result of unused hotel rooms. Who will be blamed for that? Was that dishonest or just fumbling? It is hard to distinguish.
The $6 million was probably appropriated for a specific purpose. We will find this out in a couple of years when it is looked at by the Auditor General and the Public Accounts committee. It seems to me there is a prima facie case of appropriating funds for one purpose and using it for another. The Auditor General and the Public Accounts committee have been very explicit that funds appropriated for one purpose are not to be used for another. We will have to wait for the answer to that one.
The Minister of Justice will not be here then. As for myself, I plan to be here for a good long time because the people of Canada need watchdogs like myself with a government like this in power.
The $200,000 gift is not the only item about which the government has been dishonest. Earlier the Minister of Justice went to Victoria and made a magnanimous gift of $150 million

January 24, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
to the premier of British Columbia. It was all over the front pages.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext: British Columbia never had such good representation.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
Of course British Columbia needs that money. They welcomed getting it-back. However, the minister makes it sound as though he were bringing that money from eastern Canada to British Columbia by the truckload in order to make them a gift.
The people of British Columbia know where that money came from. They do not appreciate having it made to appear as though it is a gift from the great gods across the floor. I commend the Minister of Justice for his decision to quit this place early. It saves the voters the trouble of doing it for him.
There may be some discussion about the examples of dishonesty I have given. I have another piece of paper here which directly involves the Minister of Justice. It is a four page handbill entitled "The Redevelopment of Granville Island and False Creek in Vancouver".

speechtext: Order, please. I have been following the interesting remarks of the hon. member. However, I have difficulty relating those remarks to Bill C-18 which is before us, the amendments proposed to the Anti-Inflation Act and the guidelines.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
I apologize to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House if I have strayed slightly from the tenor of the debate. I was merely making a preliminary lead-in to the thrust of my remarks which will deal with inflation. That is what the bill is about. It is clear that these government expenditures are inflationary. The problem is that those that I picked out are also dishonest. If I have stressed the dishonest feature of them over the inflationary feature, I apologize. I assure Your Honour I will tie that in with the debate on this bill.
As I was saying, I have a folder on the redevelopment of Granville Island and False Creek. It is not necessary to go into the history of this island at this time. Let it be said that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation acquired title to this land in Vancouver at a time when it was being used as an industrial estate. The great gods opposite decided that industrial estates should not be located close to the city where people can get to work easily. They feel they should be moved to the suburbs, which makes it more difficult for people. They decided this should be a people place, not an industrial estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
In addition, they had to find a job for the past president of the Liberal party of British Columbia. For the past four or five years he has been the chairman, manager or director of the agency in charge of the redevelopment of Granville Island.
In order to buy up leases and clean the place up, $25 million was allocated. A park was put here and there as well as restaurants, and now they are going to put in some stores.

What is wrong with that? It is a people place at the end of a two-lane dead-end road. How many people can get down such a road? What if there were an emergency? There would be a real traffic problem.
That is a dishonest use of the taxpayer's money, money which was obtained from people in British Columbia and is now back there. The people of British Columbia were not asked whether they wanted this.
After four years and the spending of $6 million, a public meeting was finally held last December 8 to outline the plans. The results were predictable. Vancouver merchants within a mile or two of that place asked what the government was doing with their tax dollars buy building a government-owned and subsidized shopping centre to compete with them. The people of Vancouver do not want to go to this people place with the inconvenience built into it. The merchants who pay the taxes are seeing their money being used in order that the government may compete with them. With a financial policy like that, I do not know where we are headed.
Something else in our society that is inflationary is the Unemployment Insurance Commission. That may sound strange. However, that commission will spend approximately $4.4 billion this year, which is about 10 per cent of the federal budget for the whole year. It may be called an insurance fund, but the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has no interest or desire in seeing that it operates as an insurance fund. He is only interested in paying the unemployed people provided to him by the Minister of Finance. It is like a con game-"You give me the bodies and I will pay them."
However, there happens to be the matter of a shortfall in the unemployment insurance fund. The government says it is not too great. It is nearly $2 billion. The Minister of Employment and Immigration does not consider that a deficit. In answers to questions in this House, that minister said on two occasions that this is a commitment, not a deficit. Of course it is a commitment. No one would argue with that. The government instituted the unemployment insurance program. Therefore it is committed to pay those who qualify for the benefits. But it is also a deficit. It is no wonder the Minister of Finance does not know how to balance the budget when the Minister of Employment and Immigration denies it is a deficit and the Minister of Justice thinks it is proper to take money out of someone's pocket, give it back to him, and ask for thanks.
All through this inflationary period the government has been asking Canadians to tighten their belts. But there is no evidence at all that the government has been tightening its belt in turn, and the result has been further inflationary pressure.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration has made a big thing about his make-work programs. No doubt the people who are unemployed enjoy very much getting grants under the Canada Works Program and similar programs. Nevertheless, in my view the government should recognize that, if there is a need, adequate measures should be taken to meet it, and it is
January 24, 1978

clear that the need for jobs has in no way been met by any of the minister's make-work programs. The money goes out, it is spent, and it is gone; the people are back on the unemployment rolls. All that has happened is the creation of yet another bureaucracy to administer these programs-programs which meet about 10 per cent of the demand. If there is a need, let us meet it. The government ought not to give the impression that they are good fellows handing out money so as to find work for the unemployed, and so on, when at the end there is no left-over benefit.
It is a little like the situation with regard to old age security and guaranteed income supplements. The amount presently paid out to a single person is about $3,000 a year. I have not seen the latest figures but in round numbers let us say the poverty level has been placed at $6,000 a year. How can the government suggest it is really meeting the need when $6,000 is the poverty level and it pays out $3,000?
I am sorry the Minister of Justice has left the chamber because I had another item I wanted to show him. This, too, is from the Vancouver Sun-an article written last week headed "Where your money goes". The headline reads; "Basford will get $112,000 at age 75". The article goes on to say that the minister, who, as we know, is retiring, will be getting a certain pension, and explains that with built-in escalation that pension could reach $112,000 by the time he is 75.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and the other members of the House, that the minister will need that $112,000 if he should happen to live to the age of 75. He will need it because when, at the age of 75, he goes to buy his new automobile he will need not $5,000 but $60,000 in 2007, or whatever the year is 29 years from now. That price is based upon inflation continuing at its present rate in Canada-it is presently 9 per cent though there are indications it will probably end up being 9.5 per cent. If we were fortunate enough to be able to contain inflation at the rate of 7 per cent the minister would only have to pay $35,000 for his car. The point is, though, that he will need the amount of pension the papers say he is going to get.
Here are a few more examples of what things will cost: a 60-cent loaf of bread at today's price will cost the minister $7.35 when he reaches 75 taking current rates of inflation into account. If he needs to call in a plumber to fix his kitchen sink, instead of a $25 charge for a house call he will be paying $233 to get the plumber to come over for an hour.
While we are talking about inflationary pressures caused by government spending I should like members opposite to consider the case of the elderly couple getting full old age security benefits and guaranteed income supplement. I am sure hon. members to my left will be interested in these figures, particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) because he is familiar with the problems of these pensioners who are now getting $498 a month. I am sure he will be delighted to hear that when the Minister of Justice is 75 in 29 years from now, old age pensioners such as I have described will be getting $4,640 a month.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Anti-Inflation Act

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
That is $55,000 a year, which is about half of what the minister will be getting at that time. I submit the minister is not being unreasonable in signing up for his pension in these circumstances. Indeed, I am not at all sure that just being twice as well off as a couple living on old age security benefits will provide an adequate standard of living for him. If nothing is done about reducing present rates of inflation, this is exactly what we shall be seeing.
The figures I have given are not excessive. They are based on present rates of inflation and the indications are that the trend is worsening-that inflation in Canada is actually on the rise. Unfortunately, the government, and, I am sad to say, many parliamentarians do not address themselves to the real problem. It is not the amount of the minister's pension or prices in themselves. The problem is inflation-inflation and the economy. As I said earlier, the government has done nothing to see that the economy is put back on the rails so that it can produce the jobs it is capable of producing.
I saw another item in the paper which interested me and I should like to refer to it because it directs attention to the sorry state in which the Canadian government and people find themselves. The item refers to a comment made by one man to another as they waited in line to collect unemployment insurance cheques. One of them said, "It frightens me sometimes to realize that this administration, with its fiscal irresponsibility, is my sole means of support!" What a double problem it is for Canadians who probably want to work but cannot because of the policies of the government.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext: Or lack of them.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
We can understand it when the Prime Minister tells us he is sorry things have not been good, that he does not propose to run on his record-because it is bad-but that he will run on the hopes he has for the future. We are delighted to give the Prime Minister the chance to show us the programs contemplated by himself and his party. But here is an item from the Globe and Mail of December 14-I cut it out because it contains such a ludicrous statement to hear from the Prime Minister. He said "The government has no emergency plans to counter rising inflation and unemployment". He concedes that the rates of inflation and unemployment are rising, but he tells us that the government has no plans to change the situation. What a sad state of affairs! The economy is on a course which might well end in collapse and the government is bereft of ideas for dealing with the situation.
One might have thought that during the Christmas break members on the front benches opposite would have had a chance to restore themselves. We realize they were getting tired toward the end of the first half of that session, and the Christmas break, we thought, might have given them an opportunity to come up with some solutions to the country's economic problems. Well, Mr. Speaker, I was here in the House yesterday, the opening day of this resumed session, and I heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) ask the Prime Minister what plans the government had to reverse the

January 24, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
economic trend. Here is what the Prime Minister had to say as reported in Hansard for yesterday:
The government believes, and the statistics support it, that the economy has been stimulated in the proper fashion by this government.
If the Prime Minister believes this-and he says he does, so we cannot doubt him-he illustrates a complete lack of knowledge of what economics is all about, because many more things could be done by the government to cut down government outlays and restore a little respect to Canadians by enabling them to find jobs.
The root cause of inflation in any country is government spending and over-spending which results in government deficits. Government deficits must be covered somehow. The government can cover deficits easily. All it has to do is print more money. That does not mean turning on the presses and turning out dollar bills, but it means spreading around the credit and selling a few more bonds to the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada does not really want the bonds; neither do investors. The government must get rid of its bonds in order to cover the deficit.
Every home owner in Canada is aware of the fact that he must balance his budget. He can borrow from the bank and a few lending institutions for a while, but he cannot continuously borrow year after year as the government does. The government suggests that, because it is the government, it cannot go bankrupt. I wish that were true. The current inflationary trends, which are not being attacked by the government, are leading Canada into the same type of collapse that any business or family would encounter if their affairs were conducted in the same way as the government conducts its affairs.
As the House is aware, I am a chartered accountant. Accounting principles can be applied to household budgets as well as to national budgets. If one continues to carry out policies which are economically bad, then he must reap the penalties later on.
Canada requires increased production. That would allow for the expansion of the economy in a normal manner. The government recognizes that there is inflation. It quotes figures based on percentage growth year over year, as well as on a much lower rate of real growth. If the government wanted to be more honest when using the term "real growth", it would tell us that this is the rate of growth after inflation is deducted-inflation it is unable or unwilling to cover.
There have been various arguments concerning the causes of inflation. Some people believe that wages cause inflation. Wages may add to the problem of inflation somewhat, but the labour people in Canada are seeking to regain what was lost through the inflation the government has allowed to occur. Because the labour unions are attempting to keep up does not mean that workers are gouging the people of this country.
The government has decided that the minimum wage in Canada will increase. It wants the lowest paid workers to receive the higher minimum amount. Of course these workers have needs, but the floor the government puts under wages has

to work its way through the system. That results in higher prices for the consumer. Certainly that adds to inflation, but the point is that it was commenced by the government and not labour.
If a worker is earning $1 over the minimum wage and the minimum wage is increased by 50 cents, then he has to receive a proportionately larger amount. An increase of 25 cents in the minimum wage probably will result in an increase of 60 cents or more at the higher wage levels.
People have indicated that the government cannot control the inflation it imports. That statement is not completely true. Some of the goods Canada imports result in a greater cost to the consumer, but if Canada were more productive, then its dollar would be at a higher level than at present. If that were the case, Canadians might receive $1.08 U.S. on the Canadian dollar, which was the situation two or three years ago, instead of 90 cents today. The devalued Canadian dollar translates into a higher price of approximately 15 per cent on everything imported into Canada, which is a result of government policies. That could and should be avoided.
During the time that my party proposed a freeze some years ago, some people indicated that it would not control imported inflation. Those who said that forgot that the proposed freeze was to be implemented for a temporary period of 90 days. Any importer can control the price of his goods for that period. His orders are usually placed well in advance, and if there had been any problem, it could have been absorbed in his business.
I should like to direct a few remarks toward what can be done in order to resolve inflation. The government must have asked itself what can be done about inflation. Obviously it came up with the answer of controls, some year and a half after indicating how bad controls would be. That might be referred to as bungling or being dishonest. I would not want to say which right now. After a two-year period of application, the controls are not working. I refer to the government's "Year Two" report prepared by the Anti-Inflation Board. Under the section entitled "Fiscal Restraint", the report reads as follows:
The annual increase in federal, provincial and municipal government spending is back to 1972 levels or even lower.
As a comparison, during the first six months of 1977 the annual increase in federal expenditures was 13.7 per cent. At the same time as telling Canadians to tighten their belts and not spend so much money, the government was increasing its expenditures to the extent of 13.7 per cent. Also it might be interesting to note that the increase in municipal spending was 7.4 per cent, and for provincial spending it was 12.1 per cent for the first six months of 1977. Once again the federal government led the way in creating inflationary expenditures, while telling taxpayers to spend less.
Under the section entitled "Wages and Profits Restraint", the report indicates that at the end of Year Two of the program the consumer price index was 8.8 per cent, which was 2.8 per cent over the goal of 6 per cent. There are more current figures available since this was printed which indicate that 9.5 per cent seems to be the rate of increase for the consumer price index rather than 8.8 per cent.
January 24, 1978

The government indicates that it can overcome the effects of inflation by indexing, and now everything is indexed. Pensions, tax exemptions and so on are being indexed, which may relieve some of the hurt but does not solve the problem. Once again we find that the government is not attacking the root problem but simply applies indexing.
I already mentioned increases in minimum wages and I will not go through that again, but the end result of all these gimmicks that the government uses, such as indexing and so on, is that nobody is better off. In fact, I remember in 1974 when we were campaigning on the basis of controls, of a freeze with a selective control period following, working people would say to me, "Yes, we should have some kind of controls because my wife has had to go out to work for the first time in our marriage", or something like that. I said, "You mean that prices are increasing faster than your wages". Of course that was the problem. Costs were increasing at a faster rate than wages, and that is still true, so people are falling behind.
Now the government says, "We will put pensions up". In the case of the minister, his pension is capped at 7 per cent, so that if the government cannot force inflation below 7 per cent, he will fall behind for sure. Old age pensioners will be indexed at the rate of increase in the CPI, so they should be keeping their relative position. But I have spoken to many of them and they tell me they are not keeping their relative position; they are falling behind also.
There are many things that pensioners have to buy that are not included in the CPI which establishes the rate of increase in old age pensions. I say that it all comes back to the fact that Canada is not competitive in world markets because we have not been creating an attractive climate for industry to want to stay in Canada. That has resulted in lower export sales, resulting in trade deficits which ultimately result in the lower value of the Canadian dollar.
Why is the climate unattractive for business? I should like to refer to an article in the CA Magazine issue of November, 1977 which tells us that companies in Canada are going bankrupt at the rate of about 100 a week. The figures they gave were as of August 18. They say there were 2,602 business failures across Canada in 1977. That is bad enough, but it is also a 29 per cent increase from the previous year. The rate of losses is also higher than ever before, with unpaid debts left by the 1977 bankruptcies totalling $409 million more in the first seven and a half months than was lost in all of 1974.
We can see the inhospitable climate created by the government for business when we look at the stock market columns, which people have traditionally followed when investing their money. The problem in stock markets now is that the result of deterioration of money values has caused serious changes in the trends in stock markets. For instance, an article in the Globe and Mail last week indicates that the Toronto Stock Exchange index of 300 stocks has gone up only 10 per cent in 20 months. That would be a bad indicator for the investment community itself, but furthermore these prices are measured
Anti-Inflation Act
in dollars which have lost one-third of their value during the last decade. They say that the Canadian dollar is well on the way to losing half its 1971 buying power by 1980. How can we expect business to conduct itself in the traditional ways and to provide traditional investment shelters and so on when the government makes it so difficult for them?
Farther on the article continues:
The circumstances have inspired the Bank Credit Analyst to revive its thesis of the past ten years, that inflation of debt along with inflation of money and prices will eventually have to be liquidated by collapse into depression. Accordingly, this service, with roots in Canada, advises extreme caution in investment policy, with an eye to defence against disaster.
That writer is not the only one who has spotted the serious problem, and the flight of investment capital and expertise from Canada is surely an example of the lack of confidence felt by many of Canada's strongest and best entrepreneurs and developers, and I do not mean only land development but also development of a healthy business climate.
What we need is a return of confidence in the Government of Canada, and of course there is good reason for not having any in the group over there. Also what we need is a caring for Canada. There are many Canadians who care very much for their country and who are hanging on here at their own peril through the economic crisis into which this government is leading us. The action of a company such as Sun Life in proposing to move from Montreal to Toronto is simply another illustration of this feeling among Canadian businessmen that if the government makes it inhospitable for them to work or live in a certain area, then-at least so far in Canada-we still have the freedom to make a move to some other hospitable climate.
I think it is a very sad thing for Canada, as it is for Quebec, that a move such as Sun Life is proposing has had to be considered, but it certainly was not the fault of the Sun Life people or of the sun Life policyholders who will make the decision ultimately as to where the company can best operate. It was the fault of the government of that province which made it so difficult for a company like Sun Life to operate. It is not only company problems that are involved, it is people problems. Sun Life is run by employees, and employees do not want to live in a place where the government has taken away so much of their liberty.
I want to refer again to the CA Magazine, the monthly publication of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in Canada, which held its annual conference in 1977 in Bermuda. You might think that strange. It does not have anything to do with inflation but rather with the fact that Bermuda was chosen as the site of a meeting because it is part of the Canadian Institute. All other provinces have been the site of conferences of the Institute of Chartered Accountants, but that was the first time the conference was held in Bermuda.
The guest speaker at that conference was the new premier, the Hon. J. David Gibbons, who is also minister of finance of Bermuda. I thought his summary of his legislative intentions was very interesting, and I would like to read the following short paragraph. He said:

January 24, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
In Bermuda, we take the view that it is the government's function to make legislation that provides the right climate for the private sector, consistent with the needs of society-it should protect both the individual and the environment.
I ask the House to compare that simple statement with the attitude and performance of the government opposite. It has certainly not provided the right climate for the private sector and it has tried to interfere to overcome the resulting shortcomings of the private sector to no avail. The government has not protected the individual, who is falling further and further behind as a result of its policies and, as we hear almost daily in the House, it certainly is not protecting the environment.
These are some things Bermuda does, and I quote the words of the premier:
The right balance between freedom and control-that's how we in Bermuda see our system of government and the country's approach to economic affairs. Essentially, the Bermuda Formula boils down to a system of free enterprise, supported by the right combination of flexible controls and a minimum of legislation.
When the premier says flexible controls, he does not mean the type of controls the government opposite imposed. There are certain other things which have to be controlled in order to preserve the mood and the nature of Bermuda. For instance, ownership of cars is rigidly controlled. When there are only a few miles of two-lane road, cars cannot be allowed to block it up. Workers in Bermuda are protected, and development and construction are carefully supervised. I am sure Canadian industry thinks it has had enough of that.
I will not go through the whole list, but one or two at the end might interest some Canadians. In Bermuda there are no advertising billboards and no car rentals. However, nowhere in the Bermuda Formula, as it is called, is there anything like the government intervention in business or in the economy we know here. Bermuda has a very simple and straightforward tax system, namely, and I quote the premier's remarks again:
There's no income tax in Bermuda, nor a profits tax, nor a capital gains tax. The bulk of our revenue comes from customs duties...
This suggestion has been made by me previously in this House, and some have said that it would be a retrogressive step. However, I note that the same exemptions I suggested are allowed by the government of Bermuda. Those cover basic foods like meat, fresh fruit and vegetables. It is possible to exempt the essentials of life from duties of all kinds and still achieve a certain balance. I do not think I should dwell any longer on Bermuda or other countries. We have enough problems here.
We on this side of the House are often asked what we would propose in order to solve the problems which the government seems to be unable to solve. I would like to mention a few proposals which come to my mind. I am not in any way attempting to write our program for the next election or to commit my leader or my colleagues, but some of these ideas have been talked about, and I like them.
Tax cuts would stimulate the economy. The government might say it has cut taxes, but its own advisers have said that those cuts were not enough and were not made soon enough.
[Mr. Clarke.l
As all Canadians are going to find out when they fill out their income tax forms in April, the provinces are going to take away the $2 billion tax reduction the Minister of Finance allowed, because in negotiations between the federal and provincial governments the formula was changed. I recommend that Canadians not spend the money the minister has given us because the provinces will take a good portion of it.
In British Columbia the tax rate for 1976 was 31.5 per cent. The rate for 1977 is 46 per cent, an increase of nearly 50 per cent. I do not think we can anticipate any great stimulation as a result of the gift from the Minister of Finance.
Is a massive tax cut inflationary? I have to say no. I hope I have illustrated that the speed at which the economy turns around is not what creates inflation; it is the speed at which the government spends, and overspends, taxpayers' dollars. If a massive tax cut is not inflationary, why do we not allow it? The government says that if it did, it could not balance the budget. It says that if it cuts taxes to the extent needed to get the economy going again, there will not be enough revenue to balance the budget, and there will be greater deficits. There is a response to that, and to illustrate I will cite the example of what happened in the United States. In the mid-1950s there was what was then a massive tax reduction of some $11 billion. At the end of that particular year when revenues were totalled, it was found that the whole $11 billion was recovered in increased revenues. There was no budget deficit created as a result of giving that money back to the people. If that seems like a strange equation, let me put it in a slightly different way.
At the moment 800,000 people in Canada are unemployed. Each of them is drawing an average of $6,000 out of the treasury. These people make no contribution to the federal treasury because their incomes are too small. They are taking out all the time. If we can get things going again and if the private sector is given the opportunity to provide jobs, which it can do, those unemployed Canadians will have the opportunity to become workers and taxpayers instead of remaining a drain on the economy.
I suppose we cannot eliminate unemployment altogether, but let us suppose we could cut unemployment insurance payments by $3 billion by putting people to work. The payments amount to over $4 billion, so that would be a cut of about 75 per cent. I am sure the private sector is capable of putting those people to work if there is demand. If we are talking about a tax cut of about $3 billion, we can see that there is the possibility of having things in balance again. I know this is an oversimplification, but in a debate such as this it is only possible to leave the details for another time. After all, we are talking about policy. Instead of saying that what we have done is the best we can do, we should be doing more.
I have already talked about the inflationary aspects of government spending. The government should consider cutting its expenditures. We on this side are always asked what we would cut and are accused of criticizing the government when it does, but if we could get inflation under control, the added expenditures as a result of indexing would not be necessary.
January 24, 1978

What a boon that would be! I said earlier that the problem is not indexing. The problem is inflation, and if we can get that problem licked, the problem of indexing would also be solved. The Prime Minister said he would wrestle inflation to the ground. He therefore must think that there is some hope of getting inflation under control.
I previously mentioned the unemployment insurance deficit of about $2 billion. I think it is unfair that taxpayers who are not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits should be called upon to pick up a portion of the deficit. That deficit is an inflationary expenditure which the Unemployment Insurance Commission makes every year. Many self-employed people, retired people, young people and others who are not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits have to pay their share of the deficit.
Another matter the government might examine is the cost of operating the House of Commons. It costs $80 million a year to operate this House. That is not a big price for democracy, but it works out to about $9,000 per hour. I suppose one could say we wasted $18,000 last night with our bell ringing effort.
It is the intention of the government to increase the representation in the House of Commons every ten years until the turn of the century. Many of my colleagues ask why we need a larger House of Commons. At the moment each of us represents 85,000 or 90,000 people. Other countries have much larger constituencies. In the United States, for instance, each member of Congress represents about 400,000 constituents.
Another major area that the government should get under control is Crown corporations. Is it really necessary for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to show a loss of something like $400 million or for the Post Office to lose about $600 million? I do not know of any other business which manages to spend $2 for every $1 of revenue. The government has not given sufficient consideration to these areas.
We must ask ourselves why the government has such a lackadaisical, don't care attitude toward inflation. One reason that springs to mind is that the government itself is the chief beneficiary of inflation, so why should it do anything to control it? It borrows money in year I and pays it back in year 20 with dollars only worth half what they were in year 1. It pays interest on bonds and borrowings at about 8 per cent, which is lower than the rate of inflation, so the taxpayer is already going in the hole. Then it adds that on to his other income and charges him tax on it as well. Things are very bad for the individual but they are good for the government, so it is easy to see why the government wants to continue having inflation. It has the tools at hand, it has the controls it needs to do something about inflation, but it will not because it does not see that as a popular measure.
Last week the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs visited Washington to talk to economists there. The theme with liberal economists there was just the same-and I use the small "1" liberal advisedly. They said they had reduced inflation to 6 per cent and, although they
Anti-Inflation Act
knew that is still too high and will have disastrous results in the long run, they were advising the government not to do anything about it for a few years.
In a recent speech President Carter of the United States said that he hoped to balance the budget by 1981. Nothing that the economists could propose was seen as a politically acceptable solution to inflation. They know how to solve the problem all right, but the government will not allow them to do it. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a new government in this country would show that something could be done and something would be done.
I am afraid I have gone on for a long time, Mr. Speaker, but it is important to bring some of these points up in the debate, and I hope it will be a rousing debate that follows.
To get back to Washington for a moment, after a depressing week listening to all these liberal economists saying that they did not know what to do, or were not willing to do anything about inflation, the one bright spot was provided by the former secretary of the treasury of the United States, William Simon. It is worth noting that Mr. Simon was a long-time personal and political friend of a former minister of finance in Canada, Mr. John Turner. Mr. Simon told us that he frequently came to Canada to comfort his friend who was having a very difficult time trying to talk this government out of imposing controls. There is absolutely no doubt in my mind that the former minister of finance knew that controls would not solve our problems and that he refused to implement them. It is particularly interesting to note that not three weeks after Mr. Turner's resignation the Prime Minister announced the program of controls.
I hope I have made it clear, Mr. Speaker, that the responsibility in this matter lies with the government. As I have illustrated, using the example of the Minister of Justice, the government is not using its own money when it hands out largesse. The government is a trustee of the money it takes from the people of Canada and has a duty to spend it more wisely than has been evidenced in the last ten years or more.
Inflation must be reduced. After 2'A years of controls, however, it is increasing, as the government's own figures show. Hon. members opposite seem to think there is something strange in what I am saying, but the strange thing is that nothing has been done on that side to solve this problem which is hurting all of us and bringing the country to the brink of financial collapse.
In ten years this administration has done nothing to solve the problems of inflation and unemployment, nor the over-all economic problems in the country. It is absolutely vital that some positive action be taken if we are not to face economic collapse.

That is when he brought in wage and price controls. The bill now before us is supposed to terminate those controls over a period of time.
We now have another reversal. The controls program that has been with us since the fall of 1975 is to be dropped at precisely the time conditions are worse than when those controls were introduced-at precisely the time the statistical data for inflation and unemployment are worse than they were in the fall of 1975. This appears to be insane if you believe in the program at all.

Mr. Speaker, given the quality of that question, the hon. member will be in cabinet in two weeks. It is a gem. He asks if we are now arguing for this system of controls. Of course not. We opposed them in 1975, 1976 and 1977, and we opposed these kinds of controls in the election campaign of 1974. At least we were consistent.
The monumental capacity for hypocrisy of the Liberal party to attack the controls in 1974 was for cynical political reasons. It is worse now, and at a time when it is worse in terms of unemployment and inflation they lift the controls. If you believe in a program-that is the point I was trying to make- particularly for Liberal members of this House, if they believe in the set of controls that we now have, why in God's name take them off now? The rate of inflation, Mr. Speaker, for the last three months has been 11.2 per cent.

That is the statistical trend. The figure we got recently was 9.5 per cent year over year. What is important in economics is not a one month figure but a three month trend, and the three month trend is 11.2 per cent. I say to the Liberals, and I say particularly to the female member of the cabinet who is opposite and who is supporting the system of controls-she comes from the province of British Columbia which has concerns about inflation-how can anyone support a policy that was justified at a time when inflation was 10.9 per cent, and now say let's take it off when inflation is running at 11.2 per cent? Only the intellectual culpability of a Liberal can accept that. It just boggles the mind.
The argument made in 1975 was that unemployment which was 7.2 per cent then, was in part generated by the kind of inflation we were experiencing. Unemployment now, as everyone knows except the government, is 8.5 per cent, so it is up too. If they really believe inflation is causing unemployment, and they really believe their controls program matters a damn in terms of efficacy, they should leave it in effect and not take it off.
But of course, Mr. Speaker, every Canadian knows that with the kind of controls program we had, it had no effect on inflation at all, except there has been an impact on one part of the Canadian community. That, of course, is the impact on the wage and salary earner. The program has been reasonably effective in holding down incomes of working Canadians. It has not affected prices. Let me just give you some examples. I gave you the running rate of inflation at 11.2 per cent which means we are back at double digit inflation in Canada. What about some concrete examples? The reality is that where the government could have been effective in controlling prices, they haven't done anything. Not a thing. I will give you some prices that, if the government had been interested, could have produced a real effect on the cost of living in terms of their impact on Canadians.
Consider food prices first of all. I will concede the argument that food prices, which have been a major source of price increases in Canada, have not been subject to any realistic wage controls by a national government when those foods are imported from abroad. I will concede that. One of the reasons for opposing this particular set of controls was that you could not control imported prices. If I remember correctly, the Prime Minister said back in the campaign of 1974 that you could not control import prices. We agree with that. There are other sectors, Mr. Speaker. And I want to stress, in all seriousness that if the government had been concerned about inflation, if it is concerned about inflation now, it could move and it could do something.
With respect to house prices they are up 9 per cent year over year. My party has said "move decisively on mortgages" because if you control mortgage prices you can hold mortgages down. It does not just affect the would-be home owner, it affects the men and women who rent their accommodation, because they pay the cost of mortgages indirectly through their rent levels.

Let me state it as clearly and as succinctly, and I must emphasize, as simply as possible so the Liberals will understand it, that the New Democratic Party does indeed believe in some kinds of control program in certain sectors. In any advanced economy anywhere in the world controls have been in effect. If they knew what they were doing, a selection could be made of certain sectors of the economy and then it makes sense to interfere with the market place. What we have objected to is this abysmal set of controls which the Liberals have inflicted on the people of Canada with the only result being that of holding wages and salaries down while letting prices go up. That is what we oppose.
House prices, as I indicated, are up year over year by some 9 per cent. On a $50,000 house, which is not out of line unfortunately for a typical family buying in most urban parts of Canada, that means year over year an increase of around $4,500 in price. We have calculated that because of this government's attitude on mortgages, not moving in and holding them down, with the cumulative impact over the life of the typical mortgage with that kind of a price increase would be $12,000. A family would have to pay this amount in additional cost just as a result of the year over year increase in the price of a house. So mortgages are one sector, I repeat, not just for the home owner but for the renters, where the government could have moved in with the Bank Act and forced the banks to bring down mortgages, making changes in the regulations to ensure that the banks put up money at a low level in mortgages.
Another area of cost that affects most families in Canada is that of the energy prices. What has the Government of Canada done about that? It has allowed the oil industry, the multinationals, to charge Canadians world prices for our own oil resources. What has this meant? For example it meant that they put up by $1 a barrel the price of oil last July, with another $1 a barrel on January 1, this year. Its accumulated impact on ordinary Canadian families, we have calculated in terms of cost. The increase in cost to drive cars and heat homes has been $150 a year. That cost could have been controlled and held down. Instead of permitting oil companies to cash in on decisions that were made a few years ago in the Middle East by the oil producing cartel, instead of permitting that cartel to have its hands stretched across our border and charge Canadians these prices, we could have held down oil prices and reduced the cost of living for Canadians.
Anti-Inflation Act
Another practical matter and an area within federal jurisdiction, and where the government could have moved in on, is that of car prices. Most Canadians buy cars. Most families have them. We have an agreement with the United States that is supposed to ensure price parity between the two countries. Instead we get constant escalation of Canadian prices that are out of line with the goal of price parity. The government should have told the automotive companies that there could be no price increase this year until the prices are in line with the United States for the same products. Instead, the major manufacturers just announced they will increase their prices by 3 per cent. This will mean a $150 price increase for a typical car. Most Canadians buy their cars on time over a three-year period, paying 12 per cent or 18 per cent interest. This will increase the interest charges they will have to pay.
If the government were committed to selective action, there are a number of areas like that where it could have some real impact on prices. I refer to energy, housing, car prices, and there are others. I do not want to belabour the point this afternoon.

A Liberal member says "good". There is always a capacity for massive indigestion whenever one feeds a Liberal the truth.
I will not string out the list of particular categories of price areas that affect a typical family that could have been acted upon on a selective basis by a government committed to dealing with inflation. However, we did not have that. We had this bogus controls program which, as I said, simply ensured the restriction and inhibition of wage and salary increases for ordinary Canadians.
I will not take quite as much time as the second speaker on this bill. I would like to indicate in my comments the general direction that the New Democratic Party believes is required in dealing with an economy such as ours at this time. Although I will be brief this afternoon, this is an illustration in short form of a general policy that has been developed and enunciated in the past.
First, we believe the Government of Canada ought to recognize at long last what has been accepted by governments as different as those of Japan, France, Sweden and West Germany. Two of those countries have social democratic governments, two do not. What they all have in common is a commitment to national economic planning. Entailed in that is a sophisticated approach to developing certain industrial sectors to ensure employment. It is no accident that all of those countries I have just mentioned have unemployment rates that are not even half the unemployment level in Canada. I am saying this in the context of dealing with inflation as well.
Those countries take sophisticated counter-cyclical policies over a period of time, not to remove entirely but to try to level out the cyclical nature of market economies so that the impact of inflation is minimized. That requires a commitment to

Anti-Inflation Act
national economic planning. It requires a commitment by our national government to recognize that in terms of world competition, in times of economic forces on the global scale, our national government should play a leading role in managing the economy. That we have not had.
Second, and in relation to that, there is the very important connection between production and inflation. It is not a simple direct connection, but there is some connection. When you have a million people who are unemployed and a manufacturing sector operating at only 82 per cent capacity, your economy is not producing the goods and services which, if it were producing, would have an effect on driving down prices.
There is a connection between unemployment levels and inflation. If you had a sensibly planned economy, one that ensured investment was going into the right sectors, and you had something approaching full employment, that would have an impact on driving down prices in certain key sectors. Again, we do not have that. Instead, we have a million unemployed, the worst level since the great depression.
Third, and I gave some examples of this earlier, in our country we need a system of direct controls in certain sectors in terms of prices, either because the prices are subject to oligopolistic action by a few firms in the economy and require direct government intervention to protect the consumer, or because we believe in society the particular price of a certain commodity for its own sake ought to be controlled and held down. In the latter case, I think of something like mortgages.
If you believe that housing is a social right, as my party does, through community or government action you have to take the kind of steps we took years ago with medicare and hospitalization to make that effectively a social right. That means dealing with the banks in a tough minded way to bring down, for example, the price of mortgages. The point I make is that you need effective price control in a certain specific number of sectors. We have not had that with this government.
As a concrete measure to improve circumstances for Canadian consumers, we have recommended, on behalf of my party as recently as last week in Toronto, a reduction in the sales tax, which is regressive. It hits the poor person, whether a pensioner, an elderly person living in Cape Breton, or his or her equivalent living in British Columbia. Sales tax hits the pensioner and the millionaire. It is very regressive.
In terms of dealing with the impact of rising costs and in terms of job creation, we have recommended a reduction in sales tax. Related to that, there should be serious negotiation between the federal government and the provinces so that the federal government can compensate the provinces in some way for the lost revenue they would experience in a reduction in the sales tax.
I want to stress that reducing the sales tax is a most equitable kind of proposal because it would bring proportionately greater benefits to low income people. That is something under the present circumstances which the government should act upon, perhaps even as an interim measure.
[Mr. Broadbent.l
Finally, I want to propose on behalf of my party that we have to recognize the divergent needs and interests of the Canadian economy. We have to recognize that Canadians are prepared, and indeed want to work hard. They will be co-operative in terms of wage and salary demands if the government will set an example. By that I mean a real example in terms of bringing forward a coherent government policy, something which in other countries has been called a social compact. I cannot stress too much the relevance of that.
In Sweden, West Germany, and more recently in Great Britain, the governments of those countries know they can get wage and salary co-operation from ordinary men and women. If in certain sectors jobs are threatened and wage and salary increases are out of line, ordinary Canadians can perceive that well in advance. However, you cannot expect ordinary Canadians to co-operate with regard to wage and salary demands if you maintain simultaneously an unfair tax system that ensures great disparities in Canada. The same is true if you maintain simultaneously a housing program which ensures that the bottom 20 per cent of Canadians is inadequately housed or if you do not do anything about energy prices.
The point I am making is that in a mixed economy the kind of controls we have had are not the sensible kind. They are unfair and unworkable. We are seeing the results of that. They need to have a comprehensive approach. 1 do not care about the label. In Great Britain they call it the social compact approach. They have been doing it in other countries for some time without the label. What is important is the idea. The idea behind it is a sense of fairness to everyone.
What is so fundamentally wrong with the present set of controls? The present set of controls holds down wage and salary increases while permitting prices to go up. We cannot tolerate that kind of system any longer.
Let me illustrate by one final example the abysmal consequences of the kind of unfair thinking which lies behind this sort of controls program. The government is in the process of phasing out the controls program entirely. The major change it introduces, not in this bill but by regulation, is that it is going to permit wage and salary increases to go up in the coming year by some 6 per cent. What does this mean in terms of its impact on ordinary Canadians? It means this: if inflation is running at 11.2 per cent, as it is, and if wage and salary increases are to be restricted to 6 per cent, Canadians from coast to coast will suffer a net loss in real income. Let me give an example.
Let us assume the rate of inflation is 10 per cent. A man or woman earning $15,000 and getting the 6 per cent increase would suffer a decline in real income in 1978 amounting to $12 a week. But there is no guarantee a 6 per cent increase will be forthcoming, and in its absence the decline in real income in 1978 would be $30 a week. That will be the result of the government's program. Wage and salary earners are being left without any defence.
January 24, 1978

The government is saying to men and women, bank clerks, department store salesmen, unorganized workers in Atlantic Canada, "All you can get is 6 per cent, but inflation will continue unchecked." It is this kind of control program which the New Democratic Party will not tolerate. It is time it was brought to an abrupt end. It is time we put in its place a program which showed a commitment to national economic leadership, a program which would set out goals for employment and realistic targets in terms of reducing the rate at which prices rise.
In the months ahead, in a year in which we all expect an election, I, along with other members of my party, will be producing detailed proposals which we believe will not only bring a greater degree of efficiency to the Canadian economy but a much greater degree of justice, also.
